newsitem.title: USA: ConEd settlement changes have just begun.
newsitem.headline: ConEd settlement changes have just begun.

text.p: The changes an Administrative Law Judge proposed for Consolidated Edison Co of New York Inc's restructuring settlement are just the beginning of what is needed, intervenors told Reuters.
And state officials continue to have problems with the size of the rate reductions the settlement calls for.
"Anemic," was the description used by Chris McKenna, a spokesman for New York Attorney General Dennis Vacco.

Vacco had previously pointed out that the settlement's promise to lower base rates by $655 million over five years "amounts to a mere 2 percent cut in the company's $27.7 billion in revenues expected during tha time."
It was Vacco's objections that led the commission to call for a formal recommendation from the law judge on May 20.
"We agree with the Adminstrative Law Judge on competition, (it is) not coming fast enough," McKenna continued.

In the recommended decision released last Friday, Judge Judith Lee said the settlement Con Edison reached with the Public Service Commission staff "does not allow competition for generation and energy services."
The commission is now scheduled to begin consideration of the settlement, Lee's recommendations and intervenor comments in August.
New York State Consumer Protection Board Executive Directory Timothy Carey said he was "kind of disappointed" with Judge Lee's recommendations.
"Overall, our number one issue is rates and the judge did nothing to change" those called for in the settlement, Carey told Reuters.
Asked about her call for another 30 days of negotiations on the settlement, he said such discussions could be part of the commission deliberations.

Carey had called for Con Edison to use half of any earnings reflecting a return on equity of more than 10 percent to write down stranded costs. The settlement calls for 25 percent of any return above 12.9 percent to go toward stranded costs, 25 percent to reducing rates and 50 percent to shareholders.
Lee's recommendations "clearly improved (the settlement) but it did not go far enough", according to Enron Corp director of government affairs Howard Fromer said.
He hopes "the commission will finish the job the judge started."

Fromer also disgreed with Judge Lee's contention that the retail access called for in the settlement "appeared reasonable," adding "the burden is on the company to show why (this is) not being done faster."

Carol Murphy, the executive director of the Independent Power Producers of New York Inc, said: "I think (the commission) is going to have to modify the settlement," adding the law judge's recommendations "increase the pressure" for changes. ((-- New York Newsdesk 212 859-1610))
